purpose: The engine is the game-independent software that runs a show, and it is going toward an open-source show platform that designers who are not technical can use and technical people can extend.
A game designer builds a whole game as a pack in the design tool, never touching code or configuration files, and tunes it by changing a value, applying it and playing.

A venue installer fills in a profile of what the venue has, connects the pack's names to the real instruments in the room on one page, and runs one preflight that answers go or no-go with every line traceable.
A GM runs the show from four sections (Game Ops, Show Control, Environment, Game Admin), and the post-game report builds itself from what was captured during play.
A player taps tokens on a phone or a shared station with no account, no login, no app to install and no recorded identity unless the game designs an identification moment.

The business is one production, one kit and many games on it; a second kit or operator is not planned, but must stay cheap to start, so nothing in the engine may assume one kit, one pack or one production.

The standing rules: players' data stays on the kit; media never lives inside the pack; phones and hardware scanners stay equal; the engine holds no opinion about game design; red always means act now; the preflight states its own limits; and nothing deploys to the live machine until the owner says the new engine is ready.
A second, toy game stays in the repository for good, so every change is proven on two games and ALN stays one pack among others.

jobs.title: Run any game from its pack
jobs.meaning: The pack describes the game: its tokens and their content, modes, scoring, groups, cues, the clock, what each screen shows. The engine plays whatever the pack says, and nothing in the engine assumes ALN. Every part of the kit runs the same version of the pack and can say which. The toy pack proves the engine is generic.
roles: the game designer, whose pack is the whole game
the GM and the players, who play what the pack declares
the venue installer, who reads the pack's needs
the engine itself, which must not know ALN's words
jobs.goal: A designer builds a whole game as a pack and never touches code or configuration; whatever a designer changes is pack data, and the hardware scanner gets its rules as generated tables, never new firmware. One list names every holder; each copy shows its version, the game record carries it, and a mismatch shows at connect. The pack names media by fingerprint, checked against the bundle.
needs: The pack (capability 1) and the activation gate (capability 2): every part of the engine takes the game's tokens, rules, modes and cues from the pack, never from code; the engine refuses to start on a pack that fails the check and keeps the pack it adopted for the whole of a game; a new pack is taken up only between games, at a moment the lifecycle allows.

The second game's modules (capability 38), interaction primitives (capability 36) and the entity-field migration (capability 37): scoring models, hidden facts, multi-tap actions and even the word for a score-holder come from the pack.
The media bundle (capability 40) and the ledger retirements (capability 50): the pack names its files by a fingerprint of their contents and carries no venue-hardware name.
Hot-apply (capability 16) and the pack channel (capability 3): one complete list of every part that holds a copy of the pack. No document has this list today.
Content tooling (capability 41): a replacement for Notion feeds the same pack through the same gate.
Hardware-scanner parity (capability 49): a mechanic that needs a fleet re-flash breaks the designer's loop, so everything a designer changes is pack data.

flaws.how: The pack is read at scattered moments and no message says it changed, so the TV, the engine and a tablet can end up running different versions of one game.
The shape of the files the pack hands each device is kept by hand on both sides, so the hardware scanner cannot read the pack's own token file.
The videos and other media files the pack names are copied onto the show machine by hand, and nothing checks that every file the pack names is there.
The pack has no field that says a game runs without an engine, yet it declares a scoreboard, a clock and videos that an engine-less device cannot show.

jobs.standalone: Each device loads whatever pack copy its source holds; a tablet reloading online mid-game adopts the newest pack under the game in progress; no game record carries a pack stamp and no player device shows one. In the candidate the tablet runs the same Game rules and a Pack channel client: one pack per game, stamped on its record.
tests: Edit one token's rating on disk with the engine running and no restart: the token list, the pack file and the points a scan awards all agree, and the file's fingerprint matches the one in the engine's own list of pack files.
Connect a tablet that runs a different pack: the GM sees a mismatch on screen, or the tablet is refused.
Run the group-completion test on the real pack and on the toy pack: it runs on both and does not skip.
With no alternate pack chosen, compare the phone scanner's token file with the engine's own pack: they are the same version.

functional.people: The designer who publishes a game; the GM at doors-open; a second designer later
functional.moment: Between games when the designer publishes, and at doors-open when agreement must be visible
functional.need: The whole kit plays that game, that version, with no code change: the engine scores by it, the TV shows its words, every tablet and scanner holds the same copy, and the GM can see at a glance that they match or is refused. A second designer's game runs on the same engine.
functional.proposedTitle: The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays

jobs.shapeChange: The job is now said for the designer and for the GM at doors-open, and 'nothing assumes ALN' becomes a quality every part carries. The goal gains the Pack channel: one list of every holder, a version stamp on every copy and in the game record, compared when a device connects. The toy pack's proof moves to J10, and one needs line now takes a new pack only between games.

jobs.title: Keep one true record of the game, and show it truly everywhere
jobs.meaning: Teams, scores, claimed tokens, exposed evidence and the game's phase are each decided in one place: the engine in a networked game, the GM tablet in a standalone one. Every screen (GM tablets, the TV and other scoreboards, player devices) shows that record, also after reconnecting. J2 makes a screen right; J9 makes it say so when it cannot be.
roles: the GM, whose every decision must show the same on every tablet
the audience, who read the public scoreboards
players, in future games with hidden facts
the designer, whose hidden facts must have one home
jobs.goal: The engine's Game record decides teams, claims, scores, evidence and phase in a networked game, and the tablet decides them in a standalone one, under the same rules. Each fact reaches the screens that may see it by one route, the same live and after a reconnect, and no screen keeps a copy it judges by. The engine filters hidden facts before they leave it.
needs: The truth sweep (capability 28) and the GM scanner redesign (capability 27): a named decider for each fact the GM sees, applied to the ten service domains and the twenty-two accepted events; the redesign adds a new fact the GM writes, the game's phase.

Capture (capabilities 30 and 31): roster, notes, accusation and photos each need a decider, a place that survives a restart and a place in the reconnect catch-up. A note held only on a tablet is a copy, not a record.
The second game (capability 38) and players' phones (capability 35): hidden facts have a decider and a saved home, and the engine filters what each screen receives.
Service domains (capability 15): state and health travel together on one route, and every catch-up message carries every service. The same bug has come back four times.
Credentials (capability 12) and remote displays (capability 39): the engine knows which screens are connected and which record each may see.
Hot-apply (capability 16): every client is told that the pack changed.

flaws.how: Every tablet keeps its own list of claimed tokens that only grows, so after a delete every connected tablet keeps refusing the token the engine has freed, and a tablet that lost its connection during a Reset All Scores, and did not reload, keeps the old claims when it reconnects.
What a tablet gets when it connects and what it gets live for the same fact come from different code, so a tablet that reloaded can differ from one that watched everything happen.
Tablets and phones work out claims, points and 'seen before' from their own copy of the rules, so the result screen shows a verdict the engine has not given.
One question has several answerers inside one part of the engine or one tablet, so 'is a video playing', 'which teams exist' and 'may I scan' get different answers in different places.
Equipment state reaches the panels on a different route from its health, so a panel can look calm while the engine knows the player is down.
A reconnecting tablet infers a game boundary from whatever arrives and may wipe its own history.
After a Reset System the broadcasts are wired before the saving step, so a later Reset All Scores sends every tablet and the TV the old transaction list, and cleared evidence comes back.
A reply does not say which request it answers, so a tablet's copy and the engine's record part ways.
A tablet running a different pack than the engine is only written to a log.
Team Details reads the score from a place the tablet never fills, so it shows the wrong score while the scoreboard screen shows the right one.

jobs.standalone: Today one GM tablet holds the only copy, so tablets cannot drift, but it refreshes screens only on wired events; two standalone tablets are two separate games, and one tablet per game is undecided. In the candidate the tablet hosts the same Game record and a local Delivery; the other way is its own engine, kept equal by tests.
tests: Delete a transaction on one tablet, then rescan its token on a second tablet with no reload: the scan is accepted.
Drop a tablet's connection without reloading it, press Reset All Scores from another tablet, reconnect the first and rescan an old token: accepted.
For each fact, build the live message and the connect-time entry from the same state: equal keys and values.
Scan a token the engine will refuse: the result screen never says 'complete' and shows the engine's reason.

functional.people: The GM on any tablet; the audience reading the TV; in future games, a player with a hidden fact
functional.moment: Mid-show, at once, and after a tablet comes back
functional.need: Whatever the GM did on any tablet is what every tablet, the TV and the audience see: a delete frees the token everywhere, a reset empties every screen, and nobody has to ask which screen is right. In future games a player's hidden fact reaches only its owner.
functional.proposedTitle: One game, the same on every screen

jobs.shapeChange: The need is now agreement between screens, said for the GM and the audience. 'Decided in one place' becomes the Game record part, and who decides with no engine becomes a quality every part carries. The goal adds Delivery, one route per fact for the live change and the catch-up, and says no screen keeps a copy it judges by. The hidden-fact clause returns to the need.

jobs.title: Answer every action, and remember what happened
jobs.meaning: Every scan and every GM command gets one clear answer: done, refused and why, or try again. The game keeps a record of what was done, by GMs and by players, so the night can be reviewed, reported and captured afterwards. The two halves have different flaws and different tests; section 4 asks whether they are two jobs.
roles: the GM, who needs a plain answer to every tap
players, whose devices need to know whether a scan was kept
the owner, who reviews and reports the night
the designer, whose Review stage tells the story of the night
jobs.goal: Every request, from a tap or a button, gets one reply in one shape: which request it answers, the outcome, whether it is final and whether anything was stored. When a game ends, one record of the night is written from the facts decided during play, with roster, notes, accusation and photos captured as they happen; the report builds itself from it. Whether refused scans are recorded stays open.
needs: Two planned capabilities touch the answer: held items (capability 14), where a held cue is an answer the GM sees, and the interaction primitives (capability 36), whose multi-tap actions are requests with the same reply shape.

Capture (capabilities 30 and 31), the session-bundle emitter (capability 32), the Review stage (capability 34) and the report pipeline move (capability 33): the engine writes a structured record of the night when the game ends, from facts the engine itself decided. Nothing writes that record today.
Photo capture (capability 31): a way to receive a picture, which the engine lacks, with the data kept on the kit and retention set per game by the owner.
Held items (capability 14): a held cue counts as an answer the GM can see, with a defined end for holds caused by a broken service.

flaws.how: A reply does not say which request it answers, whether it is final or whether anything was stored, so a device deletes scans the engine never kept and replays scans that can never succeed.
When the GM ends the game, a reconnecting tablet loses its history and the wall scoreboard goes blank.

The tablet shows its own verdict before the engine answers, so the GM can see 'Transaction Complete' for a scan the engine then refuses; in a standalone game a scan into a paused game shows complete and records nothing. Whether refused scans belong in the night's record is the owner's open question, not this flaw.
The downloaded report's two totals disagree.
The device list records a hardware scanner as a phone scanner, because the route it checks in on assumes 'player' when a device sends no type.
In a standalone game nothing records what players found.

jobs.standalone: Each device's store answers and the caller ignores it: a refused scan shows Transaction Complete, the hardware scanner shows a queued scan as recorded, nothing records what players found, and starting over deletes the finished game. In the candidate the tablet hosts the same Answering, so a refusal shows, and a night's record with player scans only if delivered.
tests: Send a batch of player scans while no game exists: the engine either refuses it so the device keeps the scans, or stores them. Never 'processed' with nothing kept.
Send a batch, restart the engine, send the same batch again: the scans appear once.
End a game and reconnect a tablet: it still shows its history, its scans and Download Report, and the wall scoreboard keeps the final scores until a new game starts.
Press Skip twice quickly when the second press must fail: one success and one failure, each matched to its own press.

functional.people: The GM at a token or a button and the player at a token; the owner and the designer after the show
functional.moment: During play at every tap, and at the Review stage after the end
functional.need: At a tap on a token or a button they learn at once whether it counted, why not if it did not, or that it is held or must be tried again; nothing is silently lost or doubled. Afterwards the night's story is read from what was captured during play, not reconstructed.
functional.proposedTitle: Every tap gets its answer, and the night can be told afterwards

jobs.shapeChange: The job now rests on two parts, Answering at the tap and The night's record after the end, matching its two people and two moments; whether that makes two jobs stays question D. The goal, which spoke only of the report, now also asks for one reply shape. 'Held' and 'try again' return as outcome words, and one needs line now names the two capabilities that touch the answer.

jobs.title: Run the show's equipment, and know its true state
jobs.meaning: Video, music, sound, lights, displays and speakers do what the GM and the cues ask. The engine knows whether each is working, down, or not installed tonight, restarts what it can and lets the GM control the rest, by hand or by cue. The outside programs it drives decide what they are doing; the engine reads them, never guesses.
roles: the GM, who runs the venue from the Environment and Show Control sections
the audience, who watch the TV and hear the speakers
the venue installer, whose profile says what is installed tonight
players, whose video tokens start a video
jobs.goal: The engine reaches each outside program through one interface. The program decides what it does, and the engine dates its picture of it and checks that picture against it. One supervisor restarts a crashed program a few times, then shows a red row with a Restart button; the venue profile says whether the engine starts or adopts it. The Show runner holds what cannot run yet in one place.
needs: The supervisor (capability 9): each program gets one restart rule with bounded tries and then a red row, and the engine tells its own video or music player from a stranger's. Today four different restart shapes exist and the TV's browser has none.

The start-or-adopt setting (capability 10): a plain setting for whether the engine starts a program itself or adopts a running one, read once at start. The capability map gives it a file of its own; the candidate shape keeps it in the installer's profile. Step 3 settles which.
Self-heal (capability 11): the engine fixes a crashed program silently and raises a red row only for what it cannot fix.

Dormancy (capability 8): a not-installed-tonight verdict that sticks, silences the cues that depend on it and is never restarted, plus a decision about what a reset and a restart do to the GM's out-of-service latch.
Service domains (capability 15): no service keeps a private 'connected' note beside the shared health list, and one store for hold expiry instead of two.
Remote displays (capability 39) and the media bundle (capability 40): the engine knows whether a second screen is alive and whether the named video files exist on its disk.

flaws.how: 'Is it working' and 'what is it doing' reach the screens by different routes, so the music panel can keep a calm playing look while the engine knows the player is down.

The engine runs the video player, the music player and the sound server from a remembered picture it re-reads only in part and never dates, so the queue and the cues act on a belief that has drifted from the truth.
A Reset System leaves the music panel's feed out, so the panel is dead until a restart.
When the venue profile fails to load, six services that are installed read 'not installed', and the panel shows a calm green count.
'Is a video playing' has eight answers, and a paused video counts as not playing for four of them.

jobs.standalone: Today no venue service runs and no outside program is driven: the service panels are hidden on the tablet and each player device plays its own audio, so these flaws produce no fault with no engine. In the candidate the tablet carries Equipment and Show runner stand-ins that report every engine duty dormant, grey and never red.
tests: Play a video: the engine reports 'started' within half a second every time, whichever order the player sends its signals.
Kill the music player during play: the next push says stopped with no track, and the controls come back within about ten seconds with no reload.
Stop the lighting system, then start it again: the lighting panel shows 'unavailable', then its scene tiles, with no reload.
Pause a video, then run the queue: the paused video is not replaced, and a player who scans while a video is paused is not told the video was triggered.

functional.people: The audience who see and hear the show; the GM at the Environment and Show Control sections
functional.moment: When the game says so, and whenever the GM presses a control
functional.need: The room does what the designer cued and what the GM asked; the GM sees it happen, or sees at once that it did not and what to press; a dead program comes back by itself before anyone notices.
functional.proposedTitle: The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked

jobs.shapeChange: The need is said for the audience and the GM; 'know its true state' moves to J9, whose label every fact carries and whose goal now holds the three health words. The goal now names two parts: Equipment, which reaches each program through one interface and keeps a dated picture, and the Show runner with one held store. The host setting moves into the venue profile.

jobs.title: Move each game through its life cleanly
jobs.meaning: Setup, start, pause, end, Reset System, an engine restart, the next game and a pack change: at each moment every fact, and every copy of it, has a defined fate: kept, cleared or carried on, by one code path. J5 has no deliverable of its own; it is a table of facts against moments that every other job reads.
roles: the GM, who starts, pauses, ends and resets games
the designer, whose edit-apply-play loop runs between games
players, whose scans must not land in an ended game
the engine itself, at every restart
jobs.goal: One Lifecycle moves a game between its moments and alone resets anything; engine start, Reset System and tests share one path. Its table says what each fact keeps, clears or carries, and it tells every screen the boundary. The engine refuses a pack change mid-game, replaces a scanner's old pack at a boundary and updates only between events. Open: the table's rows, and standing cues in setup.
needs: No capability exists mainly for J5, but thirteen list it as a secondary job (the eleven in the capabilities sheet's table, plus dormancy (capability 8) and the second game's modules (capability 38), which that sheet's section 3 places here); together they ask for one table of every fact against every moment.
Hot-apply (capability 16): refused while a game is active or paused; the setup, ended and no-game cases defined.
Self-heal (capability 11): the scanner's pack copy replaced at a game boundary, once per connection and engine version.
Dormancy (capability 8) and the preflight (capability 7): verdicts recomputed at reset, at game create and at restore, and the display's health not falsely red after a reset.
The session-bundle emitter (capability 32) and capture (capability 30): every fact that exists only on a tablet reaches the engine before the game ends.
The GM scanner redesign (capability 27): the new phase fact has a defined fate at pause, end and reset.
The second game (capability 38): hidden state persists across a restart.
Blue/green cutover (capability 44): the engine updates only between events; the test environment (capability 46): reset is one code path in tests and in production.

flaws.how: Nothing says what a game boundary clears or keeps, so an ended game returns after a restart and a once-only cue stays spent into the next game.
Starting the engine and rebuilding it after Reset System are two hand-kept lists of steps that differ, so a reset leaves out the music feed and brings old data back to the TV.
A tablet that lost its connection during a Reset All Scores, and did not reload, keeps its old claims when it reconnects.
A reload restores the saved game without firing the events a live change would.
A slow reset reports failure and the new game is skipped.

jobs.standalone: The tablet decides every boundary; start, pause, end, reload, a day change and a pack change each run their own code; it opens an unnamed Active game it cannot pause or replace; the phone's seen list and the hardware scanner's queue outlive every game. In the candidate it hosts the engine's Lifecycle, or its own kept equal by tests.
tests: End a game, restart the engine, scan a player token: refused with 'no game', and the engine reports no current game.
Fire a once-only cue in game one, end it, create and start game two by the plain flow, trigger the cue again: it fires.
Run Reset System with tablets connected: every tablet at once shows an empty game with no scores, claims or history.
Scan three tokens, run Reset System, create and start a game, scan two, press Reset All Scores: the GM history and the TV evidence are empty.

functional.people: The GM who starts, pauses, ends and resets games; the designer whose edit lands between games
functional.moment: At each lifecycle button, at an engine restart, and when a pack changes
functional.need: Each act does exactly what its name says: an ended game stays ended and no scan lands in it, the next game starts clean, a restart during a show loses nothing, a pause blocks scans, and a between-games edit never reaches the game in progress.
functional.proposedTitle: Each lifecycle button does exactly what its name says

jobs.shapeChange: The need is the GM's trust in each verb rather than the developer's table; the table stays as the Lifecycle part, now the only mover and the only caller of every reset, with boot and Reset System on one path and every screen told the boundary. The goal says so; its open rows stay open.

jobs.title: Let designers build, change and try games safely
jobs.meaning: The week before the show, not the show itself. A designer edits a private draft, publishes it through the engine's own check, applies a change to a running engine between games, and rehearses on a second engine, without disturbing the live show or writing into its records. Edit, apply, play, repeat is the point of the engine work.
roles: the game designer, in the edit-apply-play loop
the owner, who designs the second game at his own pace
the venue installer, who receives the handoff
jobs.goal: Edit, apply, play, repeat; the mechanics editor and hot-apply are one deliverable. The Design studio talks to the engine by message: the engine applies a change at a window the Lifecycle allows, never mid-game, or refuses and says why. A preview engine is a second Engine instance under a preview profile, so it touches nothing live and a laptop reads hardware as not installed. Where it runs is open.
needs: The five Design pages (capability 17) and the draft and publish store (capability 4): edits touch a draft only, with the live engine's adopted version shown beside it.

Hot-apply (capability 16) and the design-iteration loop (capability 18): edit, publish, apply and play work in setup or after an end; a GM-scored trial needs a started game and so passes the start gate.
The preview engine (capability 20) and simulation profiles (capability 21): a second engine that cannot kill the live engine's programs, write into its records or mint passes it accepts.
Live verdict badges (capability 19): the same verdict function as the engine, run on the draft, labeled paper or live.
First-run state (capability 48), content tooling (capability 41) and the preset-load gate (capability 52) set no demand in the direction map's section 3.

flaws.how: A second engine on the same machine kills some of the live engine's helpers (the sound system's watcher, the TV's browser and the music player); the design-tool plan warns that a preview engine would also write into the live engine's saved records and issue passes the live engine accepts.
Publishing a pack from the config tool tells the running engine nothing; the engine scores by the change only after a restart, while a reloaded TV already shows it.

jobs.standalone: Today a standalone tablet runs no engine to rehearse against, so J6 has no shortfall of its own; a mid-game reload adopting a newer pack is filed under J1. In the candidate a published pack reaches a standalone tablet through the same Pack channel, stamped, so what the designer publishes is what that tablet plays.
tests: Publish a changed rating through the tool with the engine running: within a bounded time scoring, the token lists, the scoreboard and every tablet use it, or the engine answers that it will apply at the next window between games, or refuses and says why.
Start a second engine on the same machine while a show runs: the first engine's video player, music player, the TV's browser and the sound system's watcher are untouched.

Swap a pack mid-game and delete a transaction: scores equal what the original rules awarded, or the swap is refused during a game. Today a swap needs an engine restart, so the test swaps across a restart and keeps the game.

functional.people: The game designer; the owner designing the second game; a new designer learning from the toy game
functional.moment: In the days before a show, on a laptop or on the show machine between games
functional.need: Build a game or change one value in it, publish and apply it, and play a round within minutes; the engine's own check refuses a bad pack at the desk; nothing they do can reach the live show or its records.
functional.proposedTitle: The designer changes a value and plays it within minutes, and the live show never notices

jobs.shapeChange: The need stays the designer's and gets back the engine's own check at the desk. The goal now says the Design studio talks to the engine only by message, and the engine applies a change at a window the Lifecycle allows; the preview engine is a second Engine instance with its own names. The restart fallback in one test goes.

jobs.title: Give each person exactly what their role needs, and let each do only what their role allows
jobs.meaning: The GM gets the command center, the audience the public scoreboard, players the content of what they scan, designers and installers their tools. The engine knows who is connected, sends each screen only what its role needs, keeps private what should be private, and keeps starting, pausing, ending and score changes in the GM's hands alone.
roles: the GM, the only one who may start, pause, end or change a score
the audience, who see team scores and exposed evidence and nothing else
players, who see the content of what they scan, with no account
the designer and the installer, with their tools
the owner, whose secrets must rotate before outsiders touch the system
jobs.goal: Players never get accounts: the engine knows them by device or session id, and game data stays on the kit. Every connection shows a verified pass; the engine knows its class, name, role and whether it is there. Each screen gets what its role may see. The door checks every action once; only the GM moves the game, runs the show or changes scores. Secrets rotate before outsiders arrive.
needs: Credentials on every connection (capability 12) and auth tiers (capability 13): every connection presents a verified pass, and the floor stays operator-only.
Players' phones (capability 35): passes issued without accounts, engine-side filtering of what each phone sees, and a measured capacity for how many phones one kit carries. No number exists.
The second game (capability 38): hidden state kept from every screen except the one entitled to it.

Remote displays (capability 39): a read-only display pass issued to each display connection, never written into the page's text, capped in number and counted against the profile's number of remote displays.
The GM scanner redesign (capability 27): the GM's four sections keep working while mid-game controls change.
Open-sourcing (capability 47) and the standing safety rule: the committed lighting token and admin password rotate before any outsider touches the system.

flaws.how: A client's own word or a route's default decides whether a credential is asked for and what the station is called, so every connection gets everything and the engine cannot tell two tablets or a display from a GM.

jobs.standalone: Today no engine, pass or connection exists, so this flaw produces no fault; a tablet never set up for a networked game keeps device id 001 and is known to nobody. In the candidate the tablet carries a Connections and roles stand-in with one connection, itself, so the same door and grants run with no pass to check.
tests: Open a connection with no credential and a device type of 'scanner', then ask for the state: refused, nothing arrives.
Ask the engine for the game state with no credential from the kit network: refused, or only what a player needs.
Connect as a TV: it receives only the events its role needs, and what it receives on connecting holds only exposed evidence and team totals.
Drop a tablet's network, or kill its browser without a clean close, then reload it mid-game: it reconnects under its own station name within five seconds.

functional.people: The GM; the audience; a player with no account; designers and installers at their tools; a stranger on the venue wifi
functional.moment: At every connection and every command
functional.need: The GM alone can start, pause, end and change scores, and the engine knows which tablet did it; the audience sees scores and exposed evidence and nothing else; a player sees the memory they scanned; designers and installers reach their tools and only those; a stranger sees nothing.
functional.proposedTitle: Each person sees their part and can do only their part

jobs.shapeChange: The people now include designers, installers and the stranger, and 'the engine knows who is connected' becomes the Connections and roles part with one liveness rule. The goal adds that the one door checks every action once. One needs line now issues the display pass to a connection, never into the page.

jobs.title: Run wherever the venue and the game need
jobs.meaning: On the show machine with this venue's equipment, fitted by the installer through a profile; with or without an engine, as a choice the game declares and never mixed; and on another kit, another pack or another operating system later. Nothing in the engine assumes one kit, one pack or one production.
roles: the venue installer, who fits the game to the room
the GM running a standalone game on one tablet
players on standalone devices
a future operator with a second kit
jobs.goal: The installer picks pack and profile by path or id, fills the profile, binds each pack name to an instrument and runs one preflight. Kit names live only in the profile and the Engine instance, so new kits and machines need no code. Release checks what each machine carries at start. Phones and hardware scanners stay equal. Standalone is declared, never mixed; where, and how many tablets, stays open.
needs: Installation profiles (capability 5), the bindings page (capability 23), the hardware editor and rider (capability 24) and the Deploy stage (capability 22): the profile is read once at start, and the design says what a profile change ends in, since the pack side will have hot-apply and the profile side will not.

The start-or-adopt setting (capability 10; a file of its own in the capability map, the installer's profile in the candidate shape), the seams for more kits (capability 42) and the kit network (capability 43): no kit-unique names in engine code, per-engine names for process files, and a name server the engine reads but does not drive.
Hardware-scanner parity (capability 49): every new mechanic has matching firmware, and a decision on the hardware scanner's missing standalone mode.

Standalone games need something that says a game is standalone. Today the tablet's mode is a tap, the phone's is its URL path, the hardware scanner has no such notion, and the pack has no field for it.
The planning view (capability 25) needs nothing from the running engine.

flaws.how: Nobody declares that a game is standalone, so each device reads a missing engine as an outage, nothing says which of the pack's effects an engine-less game drops, and nothing can refuse a mixed game.
With no engine the tablet decides every boundary by its own code.
The engine and its helpers assume one engine per machine.
With no engine the tablet is the only judge and its copy of the rules has gaps.
A standalone game is drawn as an outage on every player device.
Program names and install commands are fixed to one operating-system release, so a new machine logs warnings or refuses its install.

jobs.standalone: The tablet's mode is its own tap, the phone's is its URL path, and the hardware scanner has none: it reads a missing engine as an endless outage and trails the phone in seven of 24 parity rows. In the candidate the declaration, wherever the owner puts it, reaches every device with its pack, and the tablet says standalone.
tests: In a standalone game, pause the game and scan: refused with a reason and the token not used; end the game and scan: refused.
On a new machine whose operating system gives the speaker rule and the TV's browser their new names, start the engine: it logs no warning and the TV page opens.
Start a player device with no engine in a game declared standalone: it says 'standalone', not 'offline' or 'disconnected'.
Build a clean machine from the deployment guide: it pairs a speaker and plays through it, and the install line works on the new operating-system image.

functional.people: The venue installer; a GM running a game with no engine; a future operator with a second kit
functional.moment: In the days before an event, and on the night when the engine is absent by choice
functional.need: The installer states what the kit brings tonight, binds the pack's names to real instruments and gets one go or no-go. A game declared standalone knows it is standalone instead of mourning a lost connection. A second kit or a new machine needs no change to engine code.
functional.proposedTitle: Fit the game to the venue it is in tonight

jobs.shapeChange: The title names the installer's moment; 'other kits' becomes a quality of every part, and declaring a standalone game stays here as the act J8 makes. The goal adds Release: what each machine carries is checked at start. One needs line moves the start-or-adopt setting into the profile. Question E stays open.

jobs.title: Tell the truth about what it knows
jobs.meaning: Unknown, out of date, broken and not installed tonight each look like what they are, on every screen. Red always means act now; grey means absent on purpose. The preflight answers go or no-go honestly, says what it cannot check, and labels each line paper or live. J9 makes a screen say so when it cannot be right.
roles: the GM, who must trust red to mean act now
the venue installer, who reads the preflight's go or no-go
the designer, whose editor badges use the same words as the show
the audience, whose TV clock must not count on its own
jobs.goal: Every fact and reply on a screen carries a label: how old, how sure, paper or live. Red means act now; grey means not installed or switched off; an unreadable list shows unknown. One pure Verdict, speaking healthy, down or dormant, answers the editor, the preflight and the start gate, and reaches the screen. The preflight says what it cannot check; a missing or broken profile refuses the start.
needs: One truth (capability 6) and the preflight (capability 7): unknown for an equipment list the engine cannot read; a missing or broken profile is a failed check, not 'nothing installed'; each line labeled paper or live.
Dormancy (capability 8): grey for intentional absence, so that red keeps meaning act now.
Live verdict badges (capability 19): the same words in the editor as at the show.
The truth sweep (capability 28) and screen baselines (capability 29): an audit that finds screens that say something false, and images that catch accidental change.
A reset must not leave the display row red for good.

flaws.how: Facts do not carry whether they are known, unknown, old or partial, so a screen shows a calm normal value where the truth is 'I do not know' or 'this is broken'.
A service's own state travels on a different route from its health, so a panel can keep showing an old state after the health row has changed, with nothing to say it is behind.
The engine's picture of a program carries no age.
No screen can tell 'standalone by choice' from 'engine down'.

jobs.standalone: Every device draws the missing engine as an outage: the phone says Offline all night, the hardware scanner shows a red Disconnected and a rising queue, a video token says Rescan later though that never works. No verdict says a standalone tablet is ready. In the candidate the tablet's Verdict reads every engine duty dormant, grey.
tests: Start the engine with a mistyped profile path: the tablet shows a red 'profile failed to load' row, not a green summary.
Fire a mixed standing cue with lighting dormant: the finish message and the standing-cue row name the skipped command.
Cut a tablet's connection for a minute: every live panel shows its numbers are old, and the header turns 'disconnected'.
Kill the engine: each player scanner shows offline within one poll interval, and the TV shows its clock as unconfirmed, not counting.

functional.people: The GM mid-show with seconds to decide; the installer reading the preflight; the designer reading a badge; the audience watching the clock
functional.moment: At a glance, whenever a screen is read
functional.need: Anyone can tell without asking whether what they see is current and whether they must act: red means act now, grey means absent on purpose, old looks old, the installer's go is a go and a go at the desk never passes for one in the room, the TV's clock never counts on its own, and the editor and the show use the same words.
functional.proposedTitle: Anyone reading a screen can act on it without a second question

jobs.shapeChange: J9 is now a quality with one part of its own, the Verdict. Delivery and Answering carry its label on every fact and reply, and every screen draws it. The need is the reader's glance. The goal now asks for that label, keeps the three health words that left J4, and asks the verdict to reach a screen, which today it does not.

jobs.title: Stay trustworthy as it changes
jobs.meaning: Nothing in the code or the deployment drifts unseen. Tests prove the path the show really runs; the parts that join are checked against each other; the installed pieces match; testing never touches a live show. Shipping a new version to the show, and rolling it back, sits here loosely today; section 4 asks whether this job is too big.
roles: the owner, who decides when the new engine is ready
the people building the engine, whose green run must mean something
the GM, whose live show no test may touch
jobs.goal: A ladder of test rungs, the first running the real software with stand-in equipment. Each test run, preview and second kit has its own engine names, so no test reaches a live show. Shared shapes are written once; tests check every fake against the real thing; skips are loud. Every change runs on two packs. The owner alone sends a checked machine; rollback is a replug.
needs: The test environment (capability 46): tests cannot touch the live machine's tracking files, the TV or its players; they skip loudly with a reason. Today nothing stops a test copy of the engine from starting the sound system; in the candidate shape a test engine runs as an engine of its own, with a stand-in for sound, so no switch is needed.

The seams for more kits (capability 42) and the preview engine (capability 20): the same per-engine naming layer as test runs, built once. Sixteen fixed temporary paths in eight files and two machine-wide kills exist today.
The supervisor (capability 9): process cleanup that cannot hit the wrong process.
Screen baselines (capability 29) and the two-pack run: guards against changes the owner did not choose.

Blue/green cutover (capability 44), the Block 1 deliverables (capability 45) and the Block 6 close (capability 51): frozen production and blue containment honored; nothing deploys until the owner says so.
The rig that ran the real stack was lost with the container; its recipe survives.

flaws.how: The engine names its helper files in fixed places and kills by pattern across the whole machine, and the tests adopt the real display and audio, so a test run killed the live show's video player on blue, and in today's tree the same run kills the live engine's video-signal watcher and overwrites its helper files.
Names and shapes that join two places are kept by hand on each side and nothing checks that the sides agree, so a mismatch fails silently.
The deployed game is several separately versioned checkouts, a built folder, hand-copied media and hand-run steps that nothing compares, so a rollback quietly runs a mixture.
Hand-written fakes are never checked against the real classes, skips and silent passes count as green, and coverage is counted per file, so a green run does not show the real path works.

jobs.standalone: No run covers either player device's standalone path; the phone's pack test passes on a file the deployed folder lacks; the hardware scanner's boot has no test; one cross-mode proof compares scores only and skips its group case on the real pack. In the candidate the same proofs cover the tablet; its own engine would need a cross-check.
tests: Start a live engine and run the unit tests: the music player, the video-signal watchers, the sound system's watcher and the TV's browser all keep running, and the files that track them are unchanged.
A test compares every fake with the real class it stands for and fails on a member the real class lacks or a different return shape.

Give the tests a layer that runs Reset System the way the show does (today the wiring between services is undone only under test): on it, after a reset the music panel shows the new track within a second, and a cue on video start fires exactly once. Both fail today on that layer.
Roll back the deployed game: every checkout moves, and a status check lists any that did not.

functional.people: The developer who changes the engine; the owner who sends a version to the venue; the GM whose live show no test may touch
functional.moment: Before every change reaches anyone, and on release day
functional.need: A green run means the show path still works for ALN and for the toy game; the owner decides when a new version goes to the venue, what the machine carries is one matching set, and the owner can swap back by replugging a machine; no test or rehearsal ever reaches a live show.
functional.proposedTitle: A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show

jobs.shapeChange: J10 is now a quality over every part with three parts of its own, Joins and proofs, Engine instance and Release, which split it by moment: the developer's green run and the owner's release day; question F stays open. The goal closes its open item as a candidate: one naming layer for tests, previews and a second kit. Two needs lines are corrected.

jobChanges: J1 now says that nothing in the engine assumes ALN, and that every part of the kit runs the same version of the pack and can say which. Both mapping sheets asked for one of these. Keep both?
J7 now also covers who may do what: starting, pausing, ending and score changes stay with the GM, and the stored secrets rotate before outsiders arrive. Both sheets put these rules under J7. Agree?

J8 now says a game runs with or without an engine as a choice the game declares, which are the owner's own words from decision 22. The missing declaration then has a home under J8; whether it is also a seventeenth flaw stays question 23. Agree?
J3 holds two things: answering every tap at once, and keeping the night's history for review and reporting. They have different problems and different tests. Should they be two jobs?
J8 covers two audiences: the installer who fits a game to a venue, and anyone who runs the engine in another setup, with no engine, on another kit, or in the open. Should it be two jobs?

J10 carries four kinds of work: tests that cannot hurt the live show, tests that prove the real path, checks that joined parts agree, and checks that what is installed matches. Widen its sentence to include shipping a new version, split it in two, or leave it?
The two sheets disagree about which job makes sure the equipment's state (music, video, lights) shows truly on every screen: the one-true-record job, or the equipment job. Which?
